Preparing your data

Source: vignettes/data-preparation.Rmd
data-preparation.Rmd
library(isoniche)

This vignette covers the decisions to make before estimating niche breadth: the data format, sampling effort, what counts as a replicate, which habitats to include, and what to do with incomplete or small sites.

Long format

All the main functions (check_coverage(), fit_isodars(), niche_breadth(), group_sites()) take data in long format, with one row per species x site x habitat and columns named by arguments:

argument column required
species species name no (without it the data are one species)
site replicate (site, or survey) yes
habitat habitat yes
abundance number of individuals yes
effort sampling effort no (default: 1 for every row)

Rules:

  • A habitat not sampled at a site has no row. A habitat sampled where the species was not found has a row with abundance 0. If any species has a row for a site and habitat, that site and habitat count as sampled, and missing rows of other species there are treated as 0.
  • There is at most one row per species, site and habitat; pool repeated samples first (see below).
  • Sites where a species has no individuals at all are dropped for that species: they carry no information on how it distributes among habitats.
  • If habitat is a factor, its levels set the order of habitats.

From a community matrix

Community data are often stored as a matrix of samples x species, with a separate table of sample attributes. community_to_long() converts them, pooling samples from the same site and habitat and summing their effort:

comm <- matrix(c(12, 0, 3,
                  8, 2, 0,
                  5, 1, 1,
                  0, 5, 9,
                  2, 7, 4),
               nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE,
               dimnames = list(NULL, c("sp_a", "sp_b", "sp_c")))
samples <- data.frame(site = c("north", "north", "north", "south", "south"),
                      habitat = c("reef", "reef", "lagoon", "reef", "lagoon"),
                      area_m2 = c(100, 50, 100, 100, 100),
                      lon = c(-149.80, -149.80, -149.80, -149.85, -149.85),
                      lat = c(-17.48, -17.48, -17.48, -17.55, -17.55))
long <- community_to_long(comm, samples, site = "site", habitat = "habitat",
                          effort = "area_m2", keep = c("lon", "lat"))
long
#> # A tibble: 12 × 7
#>    species site  habitat abundance area_m2   lon   lat
#>    <chr>   <chr> <chr>       <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1 sp_a    north lagoon          5     100 -150. -17.5
#>  2 sp_a    north reef           20     150 -150. -17.5
#>  3 sp_a    south lagoon          2     100 -150. -17.6
#>  4 sp_a    south reef            0     100 -150. -17.6
#>  5 sp_b    north lagoon          1     100 -150. -17.5
#>  6 sp_b    north reef            2     150 -150. -17.5
#>  7 sp_b    south lagoon          7     100 -150. -17.6
#>  8 sp_b    south reef            5     100 -150. -17.6
#>  9 sp_c    north lagoon          1     100 -150. -17.5
#> 10 sp_c    north reef            3     150 -150. -17.5
#> 11 sp_c    south lagoon          4     100 -150. -17.6
#> 12 sp_c    south reef            9     100 -150. -17.6

The result goes straight into the other functions, e.g. niche_breadth(long, species = "species", site = "site", habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance", effort = "area_m2"). Without an effort column, each sample has effort 1, so pooled cells have effort equal to their number of samples.

Effort and the unit of abundance

Isodars relate densities, so counts are divided by effort: density = abundance / effort. Effort can be area, transect length (with constant width), trap nights or any relative measure, as long as it is the same kind of measure in every row.

Densities are then expressed per reference_effort, by default the median effort of the data. This is the sampling unit in which “one individual” and all reported abundances (spillover abundance, the x-axis of niche breadth curves) are measured. DI niche breadth is evaluated where the least favoured habitat holds one individual per reference effort, so DI niche breadth and spillover abundance depend on this unit, while isodar slopes and DD niche breadth do not. Use the same reference_effort for all species you compare, and report it.

fish <- moorea_fish[moorea_fish$species == "Chaetodon ornatissimus", ]
fish$effort <- 1
unit1 <- niche_breadth(fish, site = "site", habitat = "habitat",
                       abundance = "abundance", effort = "effort",
                       n_boot = 0, diagnostics = list(n_null = 0))
unit2 <- niche_breadth(fish, site = "site", habitat = "habitat",
                       abundance = "abundance", effort = "effort",
                       reference_effort = 2, n_boot = 0,
                       diagnostics = list(n_null = 0))
data.frame(reference_effort = c(1, 2),
           rbind(unit1[c("nb_di", "spillover_abundance", "nb_dd")],
                 unit2[c("nb_di", "spillover_abundance", "nb_dd")]))
#>   reference_effort     nb_di spillover_abundance     nb_dd
#> 1                1 0.3347681                  27 0.6369444
#> 2                2 0.2742806                  51 0.6369444

With reference_effort = 2, abundances are counted per two sampling units, so “one individual” in the least-favoured habitat is a different point along the isodars: the spillover abundance and DI niche breadth change (here the spillover abundance almost doubles, but the direction and size of the change depend on the isodars), while DD niche breadth is unchanged.

The default reference_effort, the median effort of the pooled site x habitat cells, depends on how many samples happened to be pooled. Set it to a natural unit instead, for example the area of one standard transect, and use the same value for every species you compare. The unit is printed with the results of niche_breadth().

Replicates: sites or surveys

Isodars are estimated across replicates that differ in abundance. A replicate can be a site, or one survey (a year, a season) of a site; put its identifier in the site column. With several sites surveyed repeatedly, each site x survey can be a replicate (combine the two into one identifier), but repeated surveys of a site are not independent, and the bootstrap, which resamples replicates, will then give intervals that are too narrow. Pooling surveys within a site, or analysing years at a single site, avoids this.

Which habitats

Include the habitats available to the species: those it could reach. A habitat the species never uses lowers its niche breadth, so species compared with each other should be assessed over the same set of habitats. Rare or poorly sampled habitats can be merged with similar ones before the analysis.

Absent and undersampled habitats

A habitat in which a species was never recorded is treated in one of two ways:

  • absent, when the habitat was sampled at enough sites where the species occurred (absent_min_sites, default 5) and the species was found there no more than absent_max_count times (default 0). It is fixed at 0, excluded from the isodar fit and counted as 0 in niche breadth.
  • undersampled, when it was sampled at too few such sites. The zeros may then be chance, so the habitat is kept and the species is flagged.
cov <- check_coverage(moorea_fish, species = "species", site = "site",
                      habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance")
cov[cov$species == "Chromis viridis", ]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 8
#>   species     habitat n_sites n_complete n_sampled n_occupied total_count status
#>   <chr>       <chr>     <int>      <int>     <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl> <chr> 
#> 1 Chromis vi… barrie…      13         13        13         13        4617 used  
#> 2 Chromis vi… fringi…      13         13        13         11        2376 used  
#> 3 Chromis vi… outer_…      13         13        13          0           0 absent

The rule can be changed (absent_max_count, absent_min_sites), switched off (absent = "none") or replaced by naming the absent habitats (absent = "outer_slope"), in niche_breadth() and fit_isodars().

With the default absent_max_count = 0, a single individual recorded in a habitat makes it used. That one record can move the spillover abundance a long way (the species must now reach one individual in that habitat), so if a few stray individuals should not count, raise absent_max_count.

A habitat used at low abundance but predicted to be empty at high abundance is not absent: it counts for DI niche breadth and is listed in the abandoned column of niche_breadth().

Incomplete sites

Not every habitat needs to be sampled at every site. Pairwise isodars (the default, dim = "pairwise") use every site where both habitats of a pair were sampled. The n-dimensional isodar (dim = "ndim") can use sites with at least two habitats through a one-factor model (ndim_method = "latent", needs the glmmTMB package); with ndim_method = "auto" it is chosen whenever some sites are incomplete. Neither is preferred in general; when many sites are incomplete, fitting both and comparing them is a useful check. n_sites in the results counts the sites where the species was recorded; the latent fit uses those with at least two sampled habitats.

set.seed(1)
inc <- simulate_isodars(slopes = c(1.5, 1, 0.8), intercepts = c(5, 0, 2),
                        n = 60, p_missing = 0.3, format = "long")
head(inc)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   site  habitat abundance
#>   <chr> <chr>       <dbl>
#> 1 site1 hab1           15
#> 2 site1 hab2           29
#> 3 site1 hab3           28
#> 4 site1 hab4           25
#> 5 site2 hab1           21
#> 6 site2 hab3           38
niche_breadth(inc, site = "site", habitat = "habitat",
              abundance = "abundance", dim = "ndim", n_boot = 0,
              diagnostics = list(n_null = 0))[c("method", "n_sites", "nb_di",
                                                "nb_dd", "flags")]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   method        n_sites nb_di nb_dd flags                     
#>   <chr>           <int> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>                     
#> 1 line (latent)      60 0.721 0.887 di_extrapolation, reversal
#> Abundances are per site (equal effort in every site and habitat).

Grouping nearby sites

When single sites lack habitats or hold few individuals, nearby sites can be merged into larger sampling units with group_sites(). It uses complete linkage on great-circle distance, so every pair of sites in a group lies within the radius; counts and efforts are summed.

set.seed(2)
d <- simulate_isodars(1.5, 1.5, 5, 5, n = 30, p_missing = 0.3,
                      format = "long")
xy <- data.frame(site = unique(d$site), lon = stats::runif(30, 0, 0.1),
                 lat = stats::runif(30, 0, 0.1))
d <- merge(d, xy)
g <- group_sites(d, site = "site", lon = "lon", lat = "lat", radius_km = 2,
                 habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance")
head(g)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   site          habitat abundance effort     lon    lat n_sites
#>   <chr>         <chr>       <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <int>
#> 1 site1+site26  hab1           28      1 0.0247  0.0673       2
#> 2 site1+site26  hab2           64      2 0.0247  0.0673       2
#> 3 site1+site26  hab3           35      1 0.0247  0.0673       2
#> 4 site10+site15 hab1           31      1 0.00364 0.0263       2
#> 5 site10+site15 hab2           92      2 0.00364 0.0263       2
#> 6 site10+site15 hab3           66      1 0.00364 0.0263       2

The radius is not chosen automatically: choosing it to improve the results would be circular. Instead, radius_sensitivity() shows how the number of units, their completeness and the estimates change with the radius; choose a radius on ecological grounds (e.g. the scale of movement of the species) and check that the conclusions do not hinge on it:

radius_sensitivity(d, site = "site", lon = "lon", lat = "lat",
                   habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance",
                   radii_km = c(0, 2, 5), diagnostics = list(n_null = 0))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 7
#>   radius_km n_units complete_share nb_di spillover_abundance nb_dd flags        
#>       <dbl>   <int>          <dbl> <dbl>               <dbl> <dbl> <chr>        
#> 1         0      30          0.233 0.391                  23 0.734 di_extrapola…
#> 2         2      16          0.688 0.384                  36 0.489 reversal, po…
#> 3         5       7          1     0.297                  46 0.695 few_sites, d…

radius_km can also be a named vector with one radius per species.

One species in wide format

For a single species, data can also be given in wide format, one row per site and one column per habitat (NA for habitats not sampled), with the habitat columns named in hab_cols:

set.seed(1)
sim <- simulate_isodars(1.5, 1.5, 5, 5, noise = 1, n = 30)
head(sim)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>    hab1  hab2  hab3 total_abundance
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>           <dbl>
#> 1    15    27    45              87
#> 2    21    37    60             118
#> 3    32    54    87             173
#> 4    51    83   129             263
#> 5    11    23    40              74
#> 6    51    82   128             261
niche_breadth(sim, hab_cols = c("hab1", "hab2", "hab3"), n_boot = 0,
              diagnostics = list(n_null = 0))[c("nb_di", "nb_dd")]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   nb_di nb_dd
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 0.381 0.738
#> Abundances are per site (equal effort in every site and habitat).

The lower-level functions iai() and isoderr() work on fitted isodars of one species in this format; see their help pages.
